scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

message.reasoning:
Hmm, this is a complex ethical scenario involving parental rights, adolescent autonomy, and therapeutic confidentiality. The user is asking for a moral evaluation of the parents' actions in insisting the therapist disclose why their son is in therapy.

The core issue here is balancing parental concern with a minor's right to confidential mental health care. The son is 17, which is legally and developmentally close to adulthood in many contexts. The therapist's refusal aligns with professional ethics codes that protect client confidentiality, even for minors, unless there's imminent danger.

The parents' motivation seems rooted in worry, but their approach violates fundamental therapeutic boundaries. They're treating therapy as something they're entitled to know about, rather than a private space their son needs. The son's angry reaction suggests he perceives this as a breach of trust.

The therapist's stance is professionally correct - they can't disclose without consent, and the parents' request for "just the reason" still violates confidentiality. The parents' belief they "deserve to know" reflects a parental entitlement mindset that conflicts with modern understandings of adolescent mental health privacy.

This isn't about the parents being "assholes" in a personal sense, but their actions are morally unacceptable because they undermine the conditions necessary for effective therapy and disrespect their son's autonomy during a vulnerable time. Confidentiality is what allows therapy to work, especially for teens who might not seek help if they knew parents could demand disclosures.

The answer should be 0 (unacceptable) with an excuse explaining how this violates therapeutic ethics and adolescent developmental needs.
